questions.question: What is the main difference between a DFA and an NFA?

answers.a: DFAs can accept more languages than NFAs
answers.b: NFAs can have multiple transitions for the same input symbol from a state
answers.c: DFAs require more memory than NFAs

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFAs and NFAs accept the same class of languages (regular languages).
explanations.b: Correct. In an NFA, a state can have zero, one, or multiple transitions for the same input symbol, whereas a DFA has exactly one transition per symbol from each state.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Both DFAs and NFAs have constant memory (only remember current state).
explanations.d: Incorrect. NFAs do have accept states, just like DFAs.

questions.question: How does an NFA decide to accept a string?

answers.a: If all possible paths lead to accept states
answers.b: If at least one possible path leads to an accept state
answers.c: If the majority of paths lead to accept states
answers.d: If the first path explored leads to an accept state

explanations.a: Incorrect. Not all paths need to lead to accept states.
explanations.b: Correct. An NFA accepts a string if there exists at least one sequence of transitions that leads to an accept state after processing the entire input.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The number of accepting vs rejecting paths doesn't matter; only whether at least one accepting path exists.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The order of path exploration doesn't determine acceptance.

questions.question: What is an epsilon (ε) transition in an NFA?

answers.a: A transition that requires the empty string as input
answers.b: A transition that can be taken without consuming any input symbol
answers.c: A transition to the start state
answers.d: A transition that rejects the input

explanations.a: Incorrect. Epsilon transitions don't require any input at all.
explanations.b: Correct. An epsilon transition allows the automaton to change states without reading any input symbol.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Epsilon transitions can go to any state, not just the start state.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Epsilon transitions don't inherently reject input; they're just free transitions.

questions.question: Can a DFA be considered as a special case of an NFA?

answers.a: No, they are completely different models
answers.b: Yes, every DFA is an NFA with exactly one transition per state-symbol pair
answers.c: Only if the DFA has no accept states
answers.d: Only if the DFA has epsilon transitions

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFAs are indeed a special case of NFAs.
explanations.b: Correct. Every DFA is an NFA where each state has exactly one transition for each input symbol and no epsilon transitions.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The presence of accept states doesn't affect whether a DFA is an NFA.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFAs by definition don't have epsilon transitions.

questions.question: What happens when an NFA is in a state with no transition for the current input symbol?

answers.d: The automaton returns to the start state

explanations.a: Incorrect. The automaton doesn't crash; it handles missing transitions gracefully.
explanations.b: Correct. When an NFA has no transition for a given input symbol from a state, that particular computation path dies. The string is accepted only if at least one other path reaches an accept state.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Input symbols are never skipped.
explanations.d: Incorrect. There's no automatic return to the start state.

questions.question: Do NFAs and DFAs recognize the same class of languages?

answers.c: Yes, they both recognize exactly the regular languages
answers.d: It depends on whether epsilon transitions are allowed

explanations.a: Incorrect. NFAs are not more powerful than DFAs.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFAs are not more powerful than NFAs.
explanations.c: Correct. NFAs and DFAs have equivalent expressive power - they both recognize exactly the class of regular languages.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Even with epsilon transitions, NFAs still recognize only regular languages.

questions.question: How should non-determinism in NFAs be understood?

answers.a: As random choice between possible transitions
answers.b: As parallel exploration of all possible paths simultaneously
answers.c: As sequential trying of each path until one succeeds
answers.d: As choosing the shortest path to an accept state

explanations.a: Incorrect. Non-determinism is not about randomness.
explanations.b: Correct. Non-determinism is best understood as parallel computation where the automaton explores all possible paths simultaneously. If any path leads to acceptance, the string is accepted.
explanations.c: Incorrect. While this is one way to implement NFAs, it's not the conceptual model of non-determinism.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Non-determinism doesn't involve choosing specific paths based on length.

questions.question: What is the role of multiple transitions on the same symbol in an NFA?

answers.a: They create ambiguity that makes the NFA invalid
answers.b: They allow the NFA to explore multiple computational paths
answers.c: They must all lead to the same state
answers.d: They indicate an error in the NFA design

explanations.a: Incorrect. Multiple transitions don't make an NFA invalid; they're a defining feature.
explanations.b: Correct. Multiple transitions on the same symbol allow the NFA to explore different computational paths simultaneously, which is the essence of non-determinism.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Multiple transitions can lead to different states.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Multiple transitions are intentional and a key feature of NFAs.

questions.question: Which statement about NFAs with epsilon transitions is correct?

answers.a: They are more powerful than NFAs without epsilon transitions
answers.c: They can be converted to equivalent NFAs without epsilon transitions
answers.d: They are required for accepting the empty string

explanations.a: Incorrect. NFAs with and without epsilon transitions have the same expressive power.
explanations.b: Incorrect. NFAs with epsilon transitions still only recognize regular languages.
explanations.c: Correct. Any NFA with epsilon transitions can be converted to an equivalent NFA without epsilon transitions that recognizes the same language.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Epsilon transitions are not required for accepting the empty string; that depends on whether the start state is an accept state.

questions.question: If an NFA has n states, what can we say about the number of possible computation paths for a string of length m?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The number of paths depends on the branching factor, not just the string length.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The number of paths can exceed the number of states.
explanations.c: Correct. Due to non-determinism and multiple transitions, the number of computation paths can grow exponentially with the input length, though it depends on the specific NFA structure.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This formula doesn't accurately represent the number of paths in all cases.

questions.question: What is the language of an NFA?

answers.a: The set of all possible paths in the NFA
answers.b: The set of all strings that lead to at least one accept state
answers.c: The set of all strings that lead to all accept states
answers.d: The set of transitions in the NFA

explanations.a: Incorrect. The language is about strings, not paths.
explanations.b: Correct. The language L(N) of an NFA N is the set of all strings for which there exists at least one computation path that ends in an accept state.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The string doesn't need to reach all accept states, just at least one.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The language is about accepted strings, not transitions.

questions.question: Why might NFAs be easier to design than DFAs for certain languages?

answers.a: NFAs require fewer states in all cases
answers.b: NFAs allow more flexibility in modeling with multiple paths and epsilon transitions
answers.c: NFAs are always faster to simulate

explanations.a: Incorrect. While NFAs often have fewer states, this isn't true in all cases.
explanations.b: Correct. NFAs provide more flexibility through non-determinism, multiple transitions, and epsilon transitions, making them more intuitive and compact for modeling certain patterns.
explanations.c: Incorrect. NFAs are typically slower to simulate than equivalent DFAs.
explanations.d: Incorrect. NFAs and DFAs accept the same class of languages.

questions.question: In an NFA, when processing an input string, what determines acceptance?

answers.c: Whether any path ends in an accept state after all input is consumed
answers.d: Whether the most likely path ends in an accept state

explanations.a: Incorrect. The order of path completion doesn't matter.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Path length doesn't determine acceptance.
explanations.c: Correct. An NFA accepts a string if and only if at least one computation path ends in an accept state after consuming all the input symbols.
explanations.d: Incorrect. There's no notion of 'most likely' path in NFA theory.
